standing_assumptions:
The article is Carlson, Incerti and Aronow, ‘Dyadic Clustering in International Relations’, Political Analysis 32:186–198 (2024). Printed page = PDF page + 185 (printed p. 191 is PDF p. 6). Everything quoted below and in the targets was read from the rendered page images (staged/pages/p-NN.png and the publisher-supplement page images, checked against 170–220 dpi renderings of staged/main.pdf and of the supplement). The paper has no numbered theorem, proposition, lemma or equation; its formal content is two displays in Section 2.1, the sandwich displays and the decomposition display in Section 3, and Tables 2–4. It writes $\mathrm{V}[\cdot]$ for variance, $\mathrm{E}[\cdot]$ for expectation and a superscript $T$ for transpose.
(S1) Model, p. 189 (PDF p. 4), Section 3: “To ease exposition, we consider the linear model of $Y_{ijt}$ on regressors $x_{ijt}$, $$Y_{ijt} = \beta x_{ijt} + u_{ijt},$$ where $Y_{ijt}$ is the level of commerce between countries $i$ and $j$ in time period or observation $t$ and $\beta$ is the slope that we obtain from fitting this model to the entire population. Under the exogeneity condition $\mathrm{E}[u_{ijt}\,|\,x_{ijt}] = 0$ and the usual regularity conditions, the parameters of this model can be estimated using ordinary least squares.”
(S2) Sandwich and plug-in estimator, p. 189: “Generically, the variance of an estimated parameter from a linear model can be represented in a symmetric form that resembles a sandwich, with two identical “bread” matrices and a “meat” matrix multiplied together in the order of bread, meat, and bread again (Aronow and Miller 2019; Davidson and MacKinnon 2004; Greene 2002): $$V_{sandwich} = (X^TX)^{-1}X^T\Omega X(X^TX)^{-1},$$ where $X$ denotes the matrix of regressors, and $\Omega$ is the variance–covariance matrix of model errors, such that $\Omega_{ijt,i'j't'} = \mathrm{E}[u_{ijt}u_{i'j't'}]$. Robust sandwich estimators are formed by assuming that some elements of $\Omega$ are equal to zero, and then substituting residuals for errors, and means for expectations. Thus, the empirical variance–covariance matrix of model residuals, $\hat\Omega$, can be plugged into the above expression of variance to arrive at a variance estimator of the following form:$^1$ $$\hat V = (X^TX)^{-1}X^T\hat\Omega X(X^TX)^{-1}.$$ So long as there is not “too much” clustering (for a precise statement, see Aronow, Crawford, and Zubizarreta 2018), $\hat V$ will be a consistent estimator of the variance–covariance matrix of the sampling distribution of $\hat\beta$.” Footnote 1: “Both the Eicker–Huber–White heteroskedasticity-consistent variance estimator and the Liang and Zeger cluster robust variance estimator are sandwich-like, “plug-in” variance estimators of this form, each making differing assumptions about $\Omega$.”
(S3) The three restrictions on $\Omega$, pp. 189–190 (PDF pp. 4–5). Naive: “The simplest case is to assume that there is no dependence across observations whatsoever in the data, which is the assumption for non-clustered RSEs: if $i \ne i'$, $j \ne j'$, **or** $t \ne t'$, then $\mathrm{E}[u_{ijt}u_{i'j't'}] = 0$, or that the errors are uncorrelated.” (Table 2; ‘or’ is bold in the paper). Repeated dyad: “The most common approach is clustering by dyad, where it is assumed that errors are correlated when $i = i'$ and $j = j'$, regardless of time period.” and “all observations in the matrix of model errors that do not share both members of the dyad are still assumed to be uncorrelated (i.e., $\mathrm{E}[u_{ijt}u_{i'j't'}] = 0$).” (Table 3). Dyadic: “By contrast, our approach only assumes independence when country pairs share no members.” and “In the matrix shown in Table 4—full dyadic clustering—we can now see that the only observations assumed to be independent are those for which the dyad does not share any members with other observations.” Tables 2–4 (p. 190) display the three patterns for six observations labelled $ijt = 111, 112, 211, 212, 221, 222$, with entries $\mathrm{E}[u_{ijt}u_{i'j't'}]$ or 0: Table 2 is diagonal; Table 3 has the three blocks $\{111,112\}$, $\{211,212\}$, $\{221,222\}$; Table 4 is zero only between $\{111,112\}$ and $\{221,222\}$.
(S4) Decomposition and DCRSEs, pp. 190–191 (PDF pp. 5–6): the display $\hat V_r = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat V_{c,i} - \hat V_D - (N-2)\hat V_0$, the sentence defining its four terms and footnotes 2 and 3 are quoted in full in P032-T11.
(S5) Reanalysis conventions, p. 192 (PDF p. 7), the last sentence running onto p. 193: “For the purposes of our reanalysis, dyads are assumed to be undirected, as modeling dyadic clustering based on directed dyads would require a stronger assumption about independence across observations.$^{11}$ Also, for the purposes of our primary reanalysis, there are no small-sample corrections made to our standard error estimates.” $N$ is not defined beside the display on p. 191; the note to Supplementary Table A.5 (supplement p. A5) says: “$N$ is the number of unique dyad members in the analytic sample.”
(S6) Terms. p. 187 (PDF p. 2): “non-incident dyads (i.e., dyads that do not share a common member)”; two observations are called incident here when their dyads share a member. KEV, p. 192: “KEVs are defined as independent variables whose parameter estimates are directly referenced in the study, or otherwise clearly pertain to the study’s stated hypotheses.” SER, p. 193 (PDF p. 8): “We compute a standard error ratio (SER) for all KEVs, which is the DCRSE divided by the standard error produced using the original variance estimation strategy.” ISFW, p. 193 and footnote 14: “where “study frequency” is the total number of KEVs for a given study appearing in the analytic sample” and “ISFW is equivalent to an average of averages across studies.”
(S7) Not in the paper. The targets index observations (records) by a single index $r$ with an unordered dyad $d_r$ of two distinct members, write $z_r$ for the bread-premultiplied score of record $r$, and call a sandwich ‘unadjusted’ when it carries no finite-sample factor. These conventions are the validators’ and are flagged where used. Every target is an exact finite statement; the two limits quoted in P032-T1 are consequences of exact identities stated there.
(S8) Which findings are targets. Of the sixteen findings rated error, five have a mathematical statement to correct or rest on an exact formal counterexample: P032-E001 (Moderate; the direction of the effect of dependence between non-incident dyads), P032-N004 (Moderate; the matrix subtracted in the decomposition for survival data), P032-E005 (Minor; the positive-semidefinite option), P032-N012 (Minor; finite-sample factors applied to Rubin-pooled matrices) and P032-E002 (Minor; a count against Supplementary Table A.2, for which the validator’s evidence is itself a Lean proof). The other eleven are not targets because their corrections change no mathematical statement: P032-E004 (an unreachable branch of the Stata command), P032-E006 (row alignment and dyad labels in the R package), P032-E008 (a selector typo that drops two KEVs; 693 for 691), P032-E009 (Supplementary Table A.3 built from the wrong result files), P032-E010 (the description of point area in Figure 3), P032-E011 (the small-sample rerun of the original standard errors), P032-N006 (the classification of Shelef 2016 as having fixed effects for both dyad members), P032-N010 (minimum Stata version), P032-N011 (an observation count in Supplementary Table A.1), P032-E003 (a cross-reference) and P032-E012 (a reference year). Of the eleven headline claims, P032-H7 (the decomposition identity), P032-H9 (the toy-example variance) and P032-H10 (the lower-bound claim, refuted by P032-E001) contain a mathematical statement; the others are empirical estimates, counts or interpretive remarks.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Introduction (p. 187), Section 3 (p. 191) and Conclusion (p. 196): the claim that with dependence between non-incident dyads ‘DCRSEs will still underestimate uncertainty’, so that the reanalysis ‘offers a lower bound’. Exact positive-definite error covariances, in bounded exogenous models, for which the dyadic restriction overstates the variance of a coefficient, and for which the residual-based DCR estimator overstates it in expectation and in the limit (the validators’ constructions; not in the paper)
canonical_claim.location: p. 187 (PDF p. 2), paragraph beginning ‘Note, however’; p. 191 (PDF p. 6), paragraph beginning ‘Note that the above approach’; p. 196 (PDF p. 11), Conclusion, first and third paragraphs
canonical_claim.statement:
Notation. Observations $r = 1,\ldots,n$; $d_r$ is the two-member dyad of observation $r$; $X$ is a fixed $n\times p$ design of full column rank; $Y = X\beta + u$ with $\mathrm{E}[u] = 0$ and $\mathrm{E}[uu^T] = \Omega$; for $c\in\mathbb{R}^p$, $h = X(X^TX)^{-1}c$; $(\Omega_D)_{rs} = \Omega_{rs}$ if $d_r\cap d_s\ne\emptyset$ and $0$ otherwise; $V_{true} = h^T\Omega h$ and $V_{dy} = h^T\Omega_Dh$ (the $c$-contrast of $V_{sandwich}$ of (S2) under $\Omega$ and under the restriction of Table 4).
(a) [Intercept, negative covariance between non-incident dyads] $n = 2$, dyads $\{0,1\}$ and $\{2,3\}$, $X = (1,1)^T$, $c = 1$, $\Omega = \begin{pmatrix}1&-1/2\\-1/2&1\end{pmatrix}$ (eigenvalues $1/2$ and $3/2$; positive definite). Then $h = (1/2,1/2)^T$, $V_{true} = 1/4$ and $V_{dy} = 1/2$, so $V_{dy} > V_{true}$.
(b) [Slope, positive covariance between non-incident dyads] Same dyads, $X = (-1,1)^T$, $c = 1$, $\Omega = \begin{pmatrix}1&1/2\\1/2&1\end{pmatrix}$ (eigenvalues $1/2$ and $3/2$). Then $h = (-1/2,1/2)^T$, $V_{true} = 1/4$ and $V_{dy} = 1/2$. So a positive omitted covariance does not give $V_{dy}\le V_{true}$.
(c) [The other direction is also possible] With $X = (1,1)^T$, $c = 1$ and the $\Omega$ of (b): $V_{true} = 3/4$ and $V_{dy} = 1/2$.
(d) [Positive dependence between incident dyads, four observations] Dyads $d_1 = \{A,B\}$, $d_2 = \{A,C\}$, $d_3 = \{D,E\}$, $d_4 = \{D,F\}$ (six distinct members), $X = (1,1,1,1)^T$, $\beta = 0$, $c = 1$. Let $u$ have the distribution on $\{-1,1\}^4$ that gives probability $3/64$ to each of the 16 points and an additional $1/8$ to each of $(1,1,-1,-1)$ and $(-1,-1,1,1)$. Then each $u_r$ has mean 0 and variance 1, $$\Omega = \begin{pmatrix}1&1/4&-1/4&-1/4\\1/4&1&-1/4&-1/4\\-1/4&-1/4&1&1/4\\-1/4&-1/4&1/4&1\end{pmatrix},$$ whose eigenvalues are $7/4$ (eigenvector $(1,1,-1,-1)$) and $3/4$ (three times), so $\Omega$ is positive definite; $h = (1/4,1/4,1/4,1/4)^T$, $V_{dy} = 5/16$ and $V_{true} = 3/16$.
(e) [The residual-based DCR estimator in the model of (d), replicated] Take $m\ge1$ independent copies of the block of (d) on disjoint sets of members: $n = 4m$ observations, intercept-only least squares, $\hat\beta = \bar u$, residuals $\hat u_r = u_r - \bar u$. The DCR estimator with no small-sample factor is $\hat V_r = n^{-2}\sum_{r,s:\,d_r\cap d_s\ne\emptyset}\hat u_r\hat u_s$ (the decomposition of P032-T11 with $N = 6m$). Writing $S_k$ for the sum of the two errors of the $k$-th incident pair ($k = 1,\ldots,2m$), $$n^2\hat V_r = \sum_{k=1}^{2m}S_k^2 - 8m\bar u^2,\qquad \mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta) = \frac{3}{16m},\qquad \mathrm{E}[\hat V_r] = \frac{10m-3}{32m^2},$$ so $\mathrm{E}[\hat V_r] - \mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta) = \frac{4m-3}{32m^2} > 0$ for every $m\ge1$. Consequently $\hat V_r/\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta)\to 5/3$ in probability as $m\to\infty$.
(f) [All six dyads among four members] Members $0,1,2,3$; the observations are the six pairs in the order $(0,1),(0,2),(0,3),(1,2),(1,3),(2,3)$; $X = \mathbf{1}_6$, $c = 1$. Let $\Omega_6$ have diagonal 1, entry $1/8$ for two distinct pairs sharing a member, and entry $-1/2$ for the three complementary (non-incident) pairs of observations: the 1st and 6th, the 2nd and 5th, the 3rd and 4th. $\Omega_6$ has eigenvalues $1/4$ (twice), $1$ (once) and $3/2$ (three times), and it is the covariance matrix of the bounded errors $$u_r = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{4}(Z_i + Z_j) + \sigma_r\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}T_{k(r)} + \tfrac12E_r\qquad(r = (i,j)),$$ where $Z_0,\ldots,Z_3$, $T_1,T_2,T_3$, $E_1,\ldots,E_6$ are 13 independent fair signs, $k(r)$ is the complementary pair containing $r$, and $\sigma_r = +1$ for the first observation of that pair and $-1$ for the second. Every row of $\Omega_6$ sums to 1 and every row of its dyadic restriction sums to $3/2$; hence $V_{true} = 1/6$ and $V_{dy} = 1/4$, while the diagonal (naive) restriction gives $1/6 = V_{true}$. With $m$ independent copies on disjoint members ($n = 6m$): $V_{true} = 1/n$, $V_{dy} = 3/(2n)$ and $$\mathrm{E}[\hat V_r] = \frac{3}{2n} - \frac{5}{n^2},$$ which exceeds $1/n$ exactly when $n > 10$, that is for every $m\ge2$ (at $m = 1$ it is $1/9 < 1/6$); and $n\hat V_r\to 3/2$ almost surely as $m\to\infty$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: (S1)–(S3). ‘Non-incident dyads’: (S6). The printed claim: P032-T5. The identity $V_{true} - V_{dy} = \sum_{(r,s):\,d_r\cap d_s=\emptyset}h_rh_s\Omega_{rs}$: P032-T2 (i)–(ii). $V_{dy}$ is the validators’ $V_D$, renamed because the paper uses $\hat V_D$ for the repeated-dyad clustered estimator; $\hat V_r$ is the paper’s symbol for the DCR estimator. For the intercept-only fit the bread is $1/n$. In (e): each block has the two incident pairs $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,4\}$; $\mathrm{E}[S_k^2] = 5/2$ and $\mathrm{E}[\bar u^2] = 3/(16m)$. In (f): with $W_6$ the $6\times6$ indicator of shared membership (diagonal included; every row sums to 5) and $q_b = u_b^TW_6u_b$ for block $b$, $n\hat V_r = n^{-1}\sum_bq_b - 5\bar u^2$ and $\mathrm{E}[q_b] = 9$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (a)–(d) and the displayed identities and expectations in (e) and (f) are exact finite statements. The two limits follow from $n^2\hat V_r = \sum_kS_k^2 - 8m\bar u^2$ in (e) and $n\hat V_r = n^{-1}\sum_bq_b - 5\bar u^2$ in (f) by the law of large numbers for independent, identically distributed, bounded blocks ($\mathrm{E}[S_k^2] = 5/2$, $\mathrm{E}[q_b] = 9$, $\bar u\to0$).
canonical_claim.note: P032-E001 is rated an error, Moderate. (a)–(c) and (f) are the first validator’s (v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 3–6); (d)–(e) are the second validator’s (v2/artifact/derivation.md, sections 3–4); both re-runs upheld. Every number was recomputed exactly when this list was fixed: rational arithmetic for (a)–(d) and the eigenvalues, full enumeration of the error distribution at $m = 1, 2$ for (e), and $\mathrm{E}[\hat u\hat u^T] = R\Omega R$ at $m = 1, 2, 10$ for (f). The examples show that the direction is not forced; they do not establish the sign of the omitted contribution in any of the 22 reanalysed studies. In (f) the naive value equals the truth while the dyadic value overstates it, which also bears on the p. 191 aside ‘although still improve over the naive approach’.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Introduction (p. 187), Section 3 (p. 191) and Conclusion (p. 196), as printed: with dependence between non-incident dyads ‘DCRSEs will still underestimate uncertainty’, and the reanalysis ‘offers a lower bound’
canonical_claim.location: p. 187 (PDF p. 2), paragraph beginning ‘Note, however’; p. 191 (PDF p. 6), paragraph beginning ‘Note that the above approach’; p. 196 (PDF p. 11), Conclusion, first and third paragraphs
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed, p. 187: “Note, however, that DCRSEs are not a panacea—the underlying theory and data generating process of the empirical setting should be taken into account prior to choosing an estimation strategy. When there is dependence between non-incident dyads (i.e., dyads that do not share a common member), DCRSEs will still underestimate uncertainty, just as only clustering on repeated dyads underestimates uncertainty when there is dependence across incident dyads. DCRSEs should therefore not be considered a replacement for approaches to clustering that (appropriately) account for greater amounts of dependence in the data. The reanalysis we present therefore offers a lower bound on the severity of the consequences of inadequate clustering practices in previous research, or, in other words, reveals the extent to which dyadic clustering *alone* is jeopardizing the reliability of research.”
As printed, p. 191: “Note that the above approach and its implementation only correct for interdependence between shared countries. DCRSEs are *not* sufficient—although still improve over the naive approach or clustering by repeated dyad approach—when there are interdependencies throughout the entire system (i.e., across non-incident dyads).” and, later in the same paragraph, “Aronow *et al.* (2018) developed conservative estimators for the variance of least squares estimators in such cases where there is further dependence—and in such cases we expect the variance of least squares estimates to be larger than those that only take into account dyadic clustering. There is therefore still a need to understand the data-generating process and underlying theory of an empirical setting prior choosing an estimation strategy.$^5$”
As printed, p. 196: “We investigated the consequences of failing to account for dyadic clustering in previous empirical research by reanalyzing all quantitative dyadic analyses in *International Organization* published in a 6-year window, thereby revealing a lower bound on the severity of the consequences of inadequate clustering practices in previous quantitative dyadic research.” and “However, solely accounting for dyadic clustering may not go far enough. For any of the studies we reanalyze, dependencies may exist in the data that extend across non-incident dyads, for example, due to network effects, in which case the problem may be even more severe than what our reanalysis suggests.”
Formal reading of the p. 187 claim (the validators’), in the setting and notation of P032-T2: for every fixed design $X$ of full column rank, every contrast $c$ and every error covariance $\Omega$ with a non-zero entry between some pair of non-incident observations, $h^T\Omega_Dh\le h^T\Omega h$ (weak form), or $h^T\Omega_Dh < h^T\Omega h$ (strict form); and, for the estimator itself, the residual-based DCR variance $\hat V_r$ does not exceed the true variance of the coefficient in expectation or in the limit. Each form is false: P032-T1.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: (S1)–(S3), (S6). $h$, $\Omega_D$: P032-T2. The corrected claim: P032-T2. Footnote 5 (p. 191) lists network-analysis approaches and is not part of the claim.
canonical_claim.note: The statement as printed for P032-E001 (error, Moderate). Per the validators the natural reading is a population or large-sample comparison, not a deterministic ordering of every realized standard error, and no standing sign restriction is stated: the same-sign condition on p. 189 belongs to the toy example (P032-T12). Not shown false: the p. 196 sentence ‘may be even more severe’ (a possibility claim, true by P032-T1 (c)) and the p. 191 ‘we expect’ read as an empirical expectation about applications. The ‘lower bound’ sentences are interpretive; the formal target is the reading above, which a formalizer can state and refute. ‘prior choosing’ is as printed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The decomposition display (p. 191) as implemented by the Stata command for survival data that are stset with an id() variable (Efrat and Newman 2016; Weisiger 2016): exact Cox example in which subtracting $(N-2)$ times the id-clustered matrix in place of $(N-2)\hat V_0$ does not give the DCR estimator (the validators’ construction; not in the paper)
canonical_claim.location: p. 191 (PDF p. 6), display for $\hat V_r$ and the definition of $\hat V_0$; dcr.ado lines 163–190; code/1_reanalysis_stata.do lines 319–334 and 347–418; Supplementary Table A.2 (supplement p. A3), rows Efrat and Newman (2016) and Weisiger (2016)
canonical_claim.statement:
Data. Ten records of six subjects on four members; a Cox model with one covariate $x$, Breslow ties, no weights or strata. Each line gives record: subject id, dyad, interval, $x$, status (1 = event; 0 = the interval ends without an event; 2 = competing event, treated as censoring).
1: id 1, $\{1,2\}$, $(0,1]$, $x = 1$, status 1. 2: id 2, $\{3,4\}$, $(0,1]$, $x = -1$, status 1. 3: id 3, $\{1,3\}$, $(0,1]$, $x = 1$, status 0. 4: id 3, $\{1,3\}$, $(1,2]$, $x = 3$, status 1. 5: id 4, $\{2,4\}$, $(0,1]$, $x = -1$, status 0. 6: id 4, $\{2,4\}$, $(1,2]$, $x = -3$, status 1. 7: id 5, $\{1,4\}$, $(0,1]$, $x = 1$, status 0. 8: id 5, $\{1,4\}$, $(1,3]$, $x = 1$, status 2. 9: id 6, $\{2,3\}$, $(0,1]$, $x = -1$, status 0. 10: id 6, $\{2,3\}$, $(1,3]$, $x = -1$, status 2.
(a) [Fit] The Breslow partial log-likelihood is, up to a constant, $\ell(\beta) = -2\log(6\cosh\beta) - 2\log(2\cosh3\beta + 2\cosh\beta)$, uniquely maximized at $\hat\beta = 0$. The risk sets are records $\{1,2,3,5,7,9\}$ at time 1 and $\{4,6,8,10\}$ at time 2, each with two events and covariate mean 0; the information is $H = 2\cdot1 + 2\cdot5 = 12$, so the bread is $1/12$.
(b) [Record scores] The efficient scores of the ten records at $\hat\beta = 0$ are $$s = \big(\tfrac23, -\tfrac23, -\tfrac13, \tfrac32, \tfrac13, -\tfrac32, -\tfrac13, -\tfrac12, \tfrac13, \tfrac12\big),$$ with sum 0; summed within subject ids they are $\big(\tfrac23, -\tfrac23, \tfrac76, -\tfrac76, -\tfrac56, \tfrac56\big)$.
(c) [Components, no finite-sample factor, $N = 4$] $V_0 = \tfrac{19}{432}$ (records); $V_{id} = V_D = \tfrac{5}{144}$ (here subject ids and repeated dyads coincide); $(V_{c,1},V_{c,2},V_{c,3},V_{c,4}) = \big(\tfrac{25}{864}, \tfrac{59}{2592}, \tfrac{89}{2592}, \tfrac{185}{2592}\big)$, with $\sum_iV_{c,i} = \tfrac{17}{108}$.
(d) [The printed decomposition] $\sum_iV_{c,i} - V_D - (N-2)V_0 = \tfrac{5}{144}$, equal to the direct sum $\tfrac{1}{144}\sum_{r,s:\,d_r\cap d_s\ne\emptyset}s_rs_s$ over ordered pairs of records whose dyads share a member.
(e) [The id-clustered matrix subtracted instead] $\sum_iV_{c,i} - V_D - (N-2)V_{id} = \tfrac{23}{432}\ne\tfrac{15}{432} = \tfrac{5}{144}$; the difference is $(N-2)(V_0 - V_{id}) = \tfrac{8}{432}$.
(f) [With the ‘asylike’ undo factor] With $n = 10$ records and $g = 6$ ids, $\alpha = \tfrac{n-1}{n}\cdot\tfrac{g}{g-1} = \tfrac{27}{25}$ and $\sum_iV_{c,i} - V_D - (N-2)\alpha V_{id} = \tfrac{103}{2160}$.
The three values in (d)–(f) are positive, so the eigenvalue step of footnote 3 changes none of them.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The display and the definitions of its four terms: P032-T11; the general identity and the general discrepancy: P032-T4. Components for scalar scores $s_r$ and bread $B = H^{-1}$ (the validators’ notation): $V_0 = B^2\sum_rs_r^2$; $V_D = B^2\sum_d(\sum_{r:\,d_r=d}s_r)^2$; $V_{id} = B^2\sum_g(\sum_{r:\,\mathrm{id}_r=g}s_r)^2$; $V_{c,i} = B^2[(\sum_{r:\,i\in d_r}s_r)^2 + \sum_{r:\,i\notin d_r}s_r^2]$. A record is at risk at event time $t$ when its interval $(a,b]$ has $a < t\le b$. With $n_t$ records at risk and $d_t$ events at time $t$ and risk-set mean $\bar x(t)$ (here 0), a record’s efficient score at $\hat\beta = 0$ is $\sum_t\mathbf{1}\{\text{at risk at }t\}\big(\mathbf{1}\{\text{fails at }t\} - d_t/n_t\big)(x_r - \bar x(t))$, with $d_t/n_t = 2/6$ at $t = 1$ and $2/4$ at $t = 2$. How the code obtains the subtracted matrix (as recorded by the validators from the staged dcr.ado): lines 164–178 re-run the command with vce(robust) and line 190 subtracts $(N-2)$ times the result times its undo factor; lines 108–119 make every record outside member $i$’s cluster its own cluster. That on data stset with id() Stata’s vce(robust) clusters on the id is taken from the Stata 15 manual entries [ST] stcox and [ST] stcrreg (runs/P032/settle/settled.json); no Stata run was made.
canonical_claim.note: P032-N004 is rated an error, Moderate: a finding about the implementation behind 13 survival models (32 KEVs; the Efrat and Newman and Weisiger rows of Table A.2, average SER 4.158 and 3.268), included because it rests on an exact formal counterexample. The printed identity itself is correct (P032-T11). The example is the adjudicating validator’s (adjudicate/artifact/proof.md, section 4; survival_records.csv); the likelihood, the information, the scores and every value in (c)–(f) were recomputed exactly when this list was fixed. Not established: the size or direction of the discrepancy in the two studies, or any corrected SER; the example is constructed and is not the original data. The validator’s second exact construction (proof.md, section 6: a least-squares design in which the eigenvalue-adjusted DCR variance ratio is 36 against a graph eigenvalue of 3) answers a separate argument about a bound and is not a target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The positive-semidefinite option of the released software (posdef in R, psd in Stata), documented as forcing the DCR variance matrix to be positive semidefinite, and footnote 3 (p. 191): exact ten-dyad least-squares sample whose DCR matrix has a positive diagonal and a negative eigenvalue, so that the option returns it unchanged (the validator’s construction; not in the paper)
canonical_claim.location: p. 191 (PDF p. 6), footnote 3; R package dcr, R/dyad_funcs.R lines 70 and 155, man/dcr.Rd and man/dcr_sandwich.Rd (argument posdef); dcr.ado lines 246–281 and dcr.hlp line 86 (option psd)
canonical_claim.statement:
Data. Ten observations, one for each dyad among five members, in the order $(1,2),(1,3),(2,3),(1,4),(2,4),(3,4),(1,5),(2,5),(3,5),(4,5)$, with $x = (3,0,2,1,-1,1,-3,-2,3,-2)$ and $y = (3,-2,-2,1,1,0,0,2,1,0)$. Fit least squares of $y$ on an intercept and $x$ (the rows of $X$ are $(1,x_k)$; coefficient order intercept, slope).
(a) $X^TX = \begin{pmatrix}10&2\\2&42\end{pmatrix}$, $(X^TX)^{-1} = \frac{1}{208}\begin{pmatrix}21&-1\\-1&5\end{pmatrix}$, $X^Ty = (4,4)^T$, $\hat\beta = \big(\tfrac{5}{13},\tfrac{1}{13}\big)^T$, residuals $\hat u = \tfrac{1}{13}(31,-31,-33,7,9,-6,-2,23,5,-3)^T$, and $X^T\hat u = 0$.
(b) With scores $w_k = \hat u_k(1,x_k)^T$, $H = \sum_kw_kw_k^T$ and $C_m = \big(\sum_{k:\,m\in d_k}w_k\big)\big(\sum_{k:\,m\in d_k}w_k\big)^T + \sum_{k:\,m\notin d_k}w_kw_k^T$ for $m = 1,\ldots,5$, the middle factor of the DCR estimator is $$M = \sum_{k,l:\,d_k\cap d_l\ne\emptyset}w_kw_l^T = \sum_{m=1}^5C_m - H - (5-2)H = \frac{1}{169}\begin{pmatrix}1984&-1108\\-1108&50\end{pmatrix},\qquad H = \frac{1}{169}\begin{pmatrix}3744&4052\\4052&15584\end{pmatrix}$$ (all ten dyads are distinct, so the repeated-dyad term equals $H$).
(c) The DCR variance matrix is $$V = (X^TX)^{-1}M(X^TX)^{-1} = \frac{1}{3655808}\begin{pmatrix}460765&-79681\\-79681&7157\end{pmatrix}.$$
(d) Both diagonal entries of $V$ are positive; $\det V = -\tfrac{70529}{308915776} < 0$; and for $c = (1,6)^T$, $c^TVc = -\tfrac{237755}{3655808} < 0$. So $V$ is symmetric with a positive diagonal and is not positive semidefinite: it assigns a negative variance to (intercept $+\ 6\times$ slope).
(e) [The gated rule] Let $\mathcal{G}(V) = V_+$ if some diagonal entry of $V$ is negative and $\mathcal{G}(V) = V$ otherwise, where $V_+$ is $V$ with its negative eigenvalues replaced by zero (P032-T7). For the $V$ of (c), $\mathcal{G}(V) = V$, which is not positive semidefinite. Multiplying by the optional small-sample factor $N/(N-1) = 5/4$ leaves it indefinite: $c^T\big(\tfrac54V\big)c = -\tfrac{1188775}{14623232}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Footnote 3 (p. 191), as printed: “To account for rare instances where negative parameter estimate variances arise due to non-positive semi-definite variance-covariance matrices, an “eigendecomposition of the estimated variance matrix . . . [that] converts any negative eigenvalue(s) to zero” and then reassembles the matrix to “force” positive semi-definiteness is performed, in line with suggestions from Cameron *et al.* (2011) and Cameron and Miller (2014).” Software documentation (read from the staged source files; there is no page image): R help for dcr and dcr_sandwich, argument posdef: “A logical value indicating whether or not DCR variance-covariance matrix is forced to be positive semi-definite.”; dcr.hlp: “psd forces the final variance-covariance matrix to be positive semi-definite.” The gate in the code: R/dyad_funcs.R lines 70 and 155, `if (sum(diag(V.hat) < 0) >= 1 & posdef == TRUE)`; dcr.ado lines 252–268, where the clipping block runs only if `Indnegvar==1`, a flag set only when a diagonal entry is negative. Decomposition and $N$ (here $N = 5$): P032-T11, P032-T4 (i). $w_k$ is the score before multiplication by the bread (the $z_k$ of P032-T4 is $(X^TX)^{-1}w_k$).
canonical_claim.note: P032-E005 is rated an error, Minor: a finding about the software’s documented guarantee, included because it rests on an exact formal counterexample to a mathematical property (positive semidefiniteness). Per the validator, footnote 3 itself is not shown false: it presents the correction as a response to negative parameter variances, which is the rule the code follows. (a)–(e) were recomputed exactly when this list was fixed, the middle factor both from the decomposition and from the direct sum over pairs. The validator also ran both unmodified R functions on these data with posdef = TRUE and obtained this matrix; Stata was not run. No reported number is shown to change. The data arise with positive probability under an exogenous model with independent errors (derivation.md, section 2).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The DCR variance under multiple imputation, corrected: finite-sample factors removed within each completed data set, DCR formed within each, and Rubin’s between-imputation term added once; with the exact gap of the pooled-first procedure
canonical_claim.location: Code only (no passage of main.pdf): code/1_reanalysis_stata.do lines 1373–1385; dcr.ado lines 125–238. The decomposition used is the display on p. 191 (PDF p. 6)
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol’s smallest repair (validated.json, P032-N012), verbatim: “Apply each component's finite-sample unadjustment only within its completed dataset (or to its pooled within-imputation covariance), form DCR, and add Rubin's full (1+1/M)B once. A general implementation computes DCR with each imputation's own sample and factors and then pools, with the intended PSD policy handled explicitly. In the fixed-factor setting without active PSD adjustment, equivalently add (1-c)(1+1/M)B to the current pooled-first covariance before PSD adjustment. Regenerate the three Schneider models and their dependent summaries.”
Formal content, with every hypothesis. Let $M\ge2$ be the number of imputations and $\mathcal{J}$ a finite index set of components with real weights $s_j$ and nonzero real factors $a_j$ ($j\in\mathcal{J}$). For each $j$ and $m = 1,\ldots,M$ let $U_{jm}$ be a real symmetric $p\times p$ matrix (the sandwich of component $j$ in imputation $m$, without finite-sample factor); let $b_1,\ldots,b_M\in\mathbb{R}^p$, $\bar b = M^{-1}\sum_mb_m$, $B = (M-1)^{-1}\sum_m(b_m - \bar b)(b_m - \bar b)^T$, $Q = (1+1/M)B$ and $\bar U_j = M^{-1}\sum_mU_{jm}$. Define $$T_j = \bar U_j/a_j + Q,\qquad T_{code} = \sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}s_ja_jT_j,\qquad T_* = \frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\Big(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}s_jU_{jm}\Big) + Q.$$
(i) $T_{code} = \sum_js_j\bar U_j + cQ$ with $c = \sum_js_ja_j$, and $T_* = \sum_js_j\bar U_j + Q$; hence $$T_{code} - T_* = (c-1)\Big(1+\frac1M\Big)B.$$
(ii) [The DCR weights] With members $1,\ldots,K$, $\mathcal{J} = \{1,\ldots,K\}\cup\{D,0\}$, $s_i = 1$ for each member $i$, $s_D = -1$ and $s_0 = -(K-2)$: $\sum_js_j = 1$. So if every $a_j = 1$ (no undo factors) then $c = 1$ and $T_{code} = T_*$: the decomposition commutes with Rubin pooling.
(iii) [The ‘asylike’ factors] With $a_i = 1 - 1/G_i$, $a_D = 1 - 1/G_D$ and $a_0 = 1 - 1/n$, $$c - 1 = -\sum_{i=1}^K\frac{1}{G_i} + \frac{1}{G_D} + \frac{K-2}{n},$$ which is not zero in general (in P032-T8, $c - 1 = -3/52$).
(iv) [Repair in this setting] $T_{code} + (1-c)\big(1+\tfrac1M\big)B = T_*$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Components and weights: the decomposition of P032-T11 and P032-T4 (i), applied within each completed data set, so that $\sum_js_jU_{jm}$ is the DCR variance of imputation $m$ and $T_*$ is its Rubin-pooled total. $K$ is the number of distinct dyad members (the paper’s $N$), $G_i$ the number of clusters in member $i$’s partition, $G_D$ the number of repeated-dyad clusters, $n$ the number of observations. Hypotheses of the setting, as stated by the validator: the same estimation sample, cluster partitions and factors in every imputation; coefficient estimates that do not depend on the variance estimator (so the same $B$ for every component); no active eigenvalue adjustment. Rubin’s rules and what the code does: P032-T8.
canonical_claim.note: Corrected statement for P032-N012 (error, Minor). Repair cost per the validator: none in the mathematics (no new sampling assumption, same estimand); an implementation change and a re-run of the three models and the summaries that use them. (i)–(iv) are the validator’s derivation (derivation.md, sections ‘Natural reading and the exact algebraic defect’ and ‘Repair, dependencies, and limits’). By (ii), pooling first is not itself the defect; the defect is multiplying Rubin’s already pooled between-imputation term by the component factors. Selecting dofundo(none) is not a repair, since it leaves the software’s factors in the within-imputation parts (validator).
